headline: AI security tool SecFoo identifies all 3 planted vulnerabilities in web app experiment
summary: An intern deliberately embedded a hardcoded credential, SQL injection, and command injection into a Python app. An AI-powered security reviewer successfully detected all three, providing context and remediation guidance.
details: Developers are discussing AI for code reviews, prompting an intern at RakFort to test an AI's ability to understand code danger beyond keywords. A small Python application was built with three deliberate security flaws: a hardcoded credential, an SQL injection, and a command injection.

The experiment utilized SecFoo, an open-source MIT-licensed CLI tool that employs AI coding agents for structured security reviews. The goal was to see if SecFoo could identify the known issues, explain the risks, and offer useful remediation.

After running SecFoo's SAST skill against the intentionally vulnerable project, the tool successfully identified all three planted vulnerabilities. The review provided valuable context, pinpointing the risky code and explaining the security concerns.

This experiment highlighted AI's potential to understand how different parts of an application interact, a capability often beyond traditional SAST tools. While traditional tools are fast and good for known patterns, AI can assess data flow and potential malicious input.

Despite its capabilities, AI security reviews are not a replacement for human expertise. A developer or security engineer is still needed to verify findings, understand application context, and confirm appropriate remediation. AI assists in investigation, but its output requires human validation.

The vulnerabilities were placed in obvious locations for measurement, acknowledging that finding more complex, deeply embedded flaws across an entire application remains a significant challenge. Developers are encouraged to experiment with SecFoo themselves.

headline_marked: OpenAI [[starts watermarking ChatGPT text]] in EU to comply with new AI Act
headline: OpenAI starts watermarking ChatGPT text in EU to comply with new AI Act
summary: The invisible watermark subtly shapes word choices, making AI-generated content detectable without affecting model performance. It's rolling out to EU users and is opt-in for global API developers.
details: OpenAI is implementing an invisible watermark for text generated by ChatGPT and Codex in the European Union. This move is to comply with the EU AI Act's transparency rules, which mandate identifying AI-generated content. The rollout for eligible EU users will occur over the coming weeks.

The watermark isn't a visible symbol. Instead, it subtly influences the model's word choices, creating a pattern that a detector can recognize. This embedded pattern travels with the text even when copied and pasted.

For developers, the watermarking feature is available today for select models via OpenAI's API worldwide, though it is off by default. OpenAI has stated it will not be a global default at launch and confirmed no meaningful change in model performance.

OpenAI also released a technical report, "textGrain," detailing the method. Co-authored with researchers from the University of Pennsylvania and Yale, it explains how secret keys sort next-word predictions to create detectable patterns.

Tests indicate the watermark can be removed by editing; replacing just 10% of words with synonyms significantly drops detection rates. Short passages, math answers, and translated text are also harder to detect.

Due to these limitations, initial detector access is restricted to approved researchers and expert organizations. OpenAI cautions that a missing watermark does not definitively prove human authorship, as text could be edited, short, or from another AI.

This announcement follows Anthropic's decision to watermark Claude-generated text globally, a move that faced some user backlash. OpenAI had previously developed a text watermark but delayed its release due to concerns about users switching to non-watermarking rivals.
